title: Michael Fagan and the Invention of Formal Code Inspection (1976)
explainer: While at IBM in the early 1970s, Michael Fagan formalized a structured process for inspecting design and code, with defined participant roles and entry/exit criteria, and reported in his 1976 IBM Systems Journal paper that it caught large fractions of defects before they reached later, costlier stages. His process is the direct ancestor of nearly every code-review practice used today, including the idea that review should be a defined, repeatable process rather than an informal favor done when time allows. Leading review well means remembering it was invented specifically to catch defects cheaply and build shared understanding, not to gatekeep.

title: Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development
explainer: Psychologist Lev Vygotsky described a 'zone' between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with the guidance of someone more experienced; later educators built on this to describe the temporary support that closes that gap as 'scaffolding.' Effective mentoring in code review mirrors this directly: a good reviewer doesn't just hand over the fix, they ask guiding questions and give just enough support that a less experienced engineer closes the gap themselves and gradually needs less help. It's a useful frame for calibrating how much to explain versus how much to let someone work out on their own.
